_doc: The modern street control every platted placement in this dataset is offset from, and the platted street module those offsets use. Until 2026-08-10 both lived only in the prose of each record's position note, restated once per building: 'the modern intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap (E …, N …) and the footprint offset 12.2 m, half an 80 ft platted street'. Five records said it, nothing checked it, and changing the module would have meant editing five paragraphs and re-doing five sums by hand. The figures here are the ones those placements actually used; tools/validate.py recomputes each placement from them (check_position_derivations) and the records declare which control they stand on.
node_rule: HOW A CONTROL POINT IS MADE FROM OpenStreetMap, written down 2026-08-10 because leaving it unwritten had already produced two wrong coordinates. A junction is the set of nodes SHARED BY THE TWO NAMED SURFACE ROADWAYS in `osm_ways`, averaged — the georeference's own rule (data/traces/gcp/hathaway_1834_gcps.json: 'multi-node crossings averaged'), since a crossing of two dual carriageways is several nodes and its centre is their mean. SURFACE ROADWAYS ONLY. Ways tagged highway=construction or proposed are not streets yet; ways under a different name are a different street, which matters here because Market Street's successor is three stacked streets (North Upper Wacker Drive, North Lower Wacker Drive, a service drive beneath that) and only the top one is the plat's; and BIKEWAYS AND FOOTWAYS ARE EXCLUDED because they are mapped a few metres off the roadway centreline, so averaging one in moves the junction centre off the streets the plat module is about. A name query written as a substring match pulls them in silently — 'Canal Street' matches 'Canal Street Bikeway' — and that is exactly what happened at randolph_canal and at kinzie_canal. tools/refetch_control.py implements both halves: --discover re-derives the node set from the names, and the default pass re-fetches the recorded ids and reports the drift. It needs the network, so it is on-demand and not part of tools/check.sh. AND THE RULE HAS A THIRD FAILURE MODE, FOUND 2026-08-27 BY T-0183 AND WORSE THAN THE TWO ABOVE, BECAUSE IT RETURNS AN ANSWER INSTEAD OF NOTHING. Two named surface roadways can share nodes WITHOUT CROSSING: where one street's modern successor CHANGES NAME INTO the other's at a bend, the shared set is the pair of nodes at the bend, and it is indistinguishable in the output from a crossing — the right count, a plausible spread, a clean mean. At Market x South Water it is not merely a different kind of point, it is 110 m from where the corner is: 'North Upper Wacker Drive' x 'West Upper Wacker Drive' returns exactly lake_market's own two nodes, because North Upper Wacker ENDS at the Lake Street junction and West Upper Wacker BEGINS there. So a --discover run that reports shared nodes is not on its own evidence of a junction: check the returned set against the control already committed, which --discover now does for you, and check that the mean is where the two streets are supposed to meet. Refusals under this rule are recorded in `refused_control` below rather than left as absences.

platted_street.note: 80 ft is the street width annotated on Hathaway 1834 and read off the sheet during the datum work; this project applies it town-wide to Lake, Market, Canal, Randolph and Kinzie. MEASURED 2026-08-10, AND THE RIVAL FIGURE IS OUT: eleven platted corridors have now been measured off the two 1834 sheets, block boundary line to block boundary line, and every one of them falls between 75.7 and 92.8 ft. None comes within 9 ft of 66. Eight of the eleven were N-S streets; the three E-W corridors added 2026-08-11 read 79.4, 81.5 and 86.5 ft, so the figure no longer rests on one axis of the grid. See `measured` below; the gate is check_street_module in tools/validate.py, which re-derives every one of those metres from its committed pixels, offline, on every commit. It stays INFERRED rather than documented and the reason has CHANGED. It is no longer that the sheet was never read street by street; it is that what has now been read is the corridor these draughtsmen DREW in 1834 — median about 4 ft wide of 80 on both sheets — while this figure claims what Thompson PLATTED in 1830. Between those two sit 3.7-4.5% of paper stretch and the placement of a pen line, so the measurement settles WHICH candidate and not the platted figure to the foot. Alleys read 17.1-18.7 ft on the same traverses, which is consistent with 18 ft and NOT conclusive against 16: two feet is inside this method's error, and a reading that cannot separate two figures does not get to pick one.

measured.note: Two traverses per sheet. Along the block row south of Lake Street: four N-S corridors on each at a centre-to-centre pitch of 116.6-123.2 m, which is the 300 ft block plus one street the plat describes and is the check that the reading is the module rather than the tool's own thresholds. Those corridors are Desplaines, Jefferson, Clinton and Canal, named from the sheets' own street labels. AND DOWN THE LOT COLUMN EAST OF CANAL, 2026-08-11: three E-W corridors on the Wright sheet, Lake at 79.4 ft and Randolph at 81.5 ft — both named by their committed modern junctions rather than by counting west from anything — and one unnamed corridor a block further south at 86.5 ft. That is the half of the reading the first pass measured and threw away, because nothing then told a Wright lot strip from a street. What tells them apart is `clear_run`: how far a candidate is open ground down its own centreline, which a strip of lots cannot be for a block face. It rejected ten lot strips on that traverse. The same traverse reads NOTHING on Hathaway — no candidate there has another a block pitch away from it — so the E-W widths rest on one sheet and are not cross-checked. See docs/RESEARCH/street_module_1830.md § 10.

dissent.note: The page at chicagology_first_post_office states that Thompson's 1830 plat laid the town out with 'straight streets uniformly 66 feet wide (the length of a surveyor's chain) with alleys 16 feet wide'. THE ATTRIBUTION WAS WRONG AND IS CORRECTED 2026-08-11: this note said 'Currey states', and the page was then read in full. The sentence is not part of Currey's 1922 article — it interrupts his post-office chronology between 1832 and 1837, it is about a survey rather than a building, and it is the one paragraph on the page carrying no authority while using diction no 1922 writer would use. It is unattributed website prose and therefore off the ladder entirely, where before it was credited to a named historian at rung 4. That does not change the outcome by a foot; it changes what was being disagreed with. See docs/RESEARCH/evidence_tiers_round_three.md § 2. NOT ADOPTED, and not averaged: an annotation on a cadastral survey sheet outweighs a narrative sentence about the town as a whole. EXCLUDED BY MEASUREMENT 2026-08-10, together with the reconciliation that was standing in for a reading. The suggestion was that the two figures are about different streets — 66 ft general, the riverfront and market streets platted wider. The eight corridors measured are the general streets of the west division (Desplaines, Jefferson, Clinton, Canal), which is exactly where a 66 ft general width would have to show, and they read 75.7-92.8 ft. So this is not a reading about other streets; it is a narrative summary that matches neither survey. It stays recorded, because a source is not deleted for turning out to be wrong. See docs/RESEARCH/hogan_store.md § 5. WHAT IT WOULD HAVE COST, kept because it is the reason the module was made one figure in one file: every offset drops from 12.192 m to 10.058 m, moving five buildings 2.13 m — an order of magnitude inside the georeference's own ±20 m, and one edit to this file rather than five.

lake.name: Lake Street
lake.note: Platted in the original town and surviving on its line, which is what makes it usable as control.

canal.name: Canal Street
canal.note: West of the South Branch. NOT West Water Street, which ran along the west bank one block east — a confusion recorded on green_tree_tavern's position.

market.name: Market Street
market.note: The equivalence is stated by this project's research dossiers and independently corroborated by the georeference, since the 1834 plats warp onto the modern centrelines at 17.5 m RMS.

franklin.name: Franklin Street
franklin.modern: N Franklin Street, unchanged name and unchanged alignment
franklin.note: Platted in the original town, still called Franklin Street and still on its own line, which is the whole reason South Water's only control point can be made here and nowhere else on that street. Named in this table 2026-08-28 with `control.south_water_franklin`.

south_water.name: South Water Street
south_water.modern: Wacker Drive, and only in part — see `refused_control.market_south_water`
south_water.note: The riverfront street of the south bank. Its modern successor is Wacker Drive, but the succession is not one line onto another: Wacker reaches South Water's platted line at Franklin and runs east on it, and WEST of Franklin it turns south-west onto the Lake and Market corner instead of carrying on to a Market intersection. IT HAS ONE CONTROL POINT SINCE 2026-08-28, `control.south_water_franklin`, at the east end of the stretch Wacker does run on — the only place on this street where `node_rule` can make a junction, and the reason the sentence that stood here until T-0245 said the street had none. West of Franklin the one derivation that was tried — Market x South Water — is recorded as a refusal below rather than as a gap. Named here because a street a refusal names should resolve in this table.

kinzie.name: Kinzie Street
kinzie.note: North of the main stem, in Kinzie's Addition rather than the original town; one of the streets that survives on its 1835 alignment, which is why the North Branch bridge's deck sits on it.

lake_canal.note: The only control point used for a placement that is also a georeferencing GCP, so its node id is recorded and its coordinate is re-fetchable. Re-fetched 2026-08-10: the node still stands where the file says, to 0.00 m. It is a single street crossing with no bikeway mapped through it, which is why it never acquired the inclusion error described on randolph_canal.

lake_market.not_corridor_control_for_note: NOT CORRIDOR CONTROL, since T-0827 (2026-09-12). This point stays exactly where it was and every placement offset from it is untouched — what it may no longer do is re-centre Market Street's PLATTED corridor under T-0009. North Upper Wacker Drive stands on ground made in 1926, when the river was walled, and T-0827 measured what that does: Market's centre to Franklin's came out 118.0-119.2 m against the plat's 400 ft module of 121.92 m, the one pitch on this grid off the module, while Wright's 1834 sheet reads 120.21 m and Thompson's own North Division tier 124.81 m. `market` is now stepped one module west of `franklin` and no longer reproduces this junction: it stands 3.30 m west of it. Re-centring the platted corridor back onto this point would put it where the ticket has just shown the street was not, which is the opposite of what T-0009 asked the re-centring to do — the ruling exists to put the corridor where the PLAT puts it rather than where a reconstruction chose to draw a line, and here the plat and the drawn line agree against the junction. The refusal is a field on the point rather than a street id in the code, so it is auditable and reversible with the evidence that produced it.
lake_market.derived_from: read from OpenStreetMap 2026-08-09 for the Sauganash placement; re-used 2026-08-10 for Hogan's store; node ids recovered 2026-08-10 by tools/refetch_control.py --discover
lake_market.note: GAP CLOSED 2026-08-10, AND NOTHING MOVED. The ids above were missing until then: the coordinate five buildings were offset from could not be re-derived from the source it names. Re-deriving the junction under the rule stated in `node_rule` gives the mean of two nodes — Lake Street crosses both carriageways of Wacker Drive's bend, 17.68 m apart — at E 447161.86, N 4637285.38, which is the committed coordinate rounded to 0.1 m, 0.04 m away. So the 2026-08-09 read is reproduced rather than corrected, and the Sauganash and Hogan's store stand exactly where they stood. The committed value is left at its 0.1 m rounding on purpose: adopting the two-decimal mean would move both buildings 4 cm for no evidential gain and for no reason a reader could see. Both nodes were last edited 2024-07-24, so nothing has moved under the dataset since it was read. Wacker Drive is three streets stacked here — North Upper Wacker Drive at the surface, North Lower Wacker Drive beneath it and a service drive beneath that — and only the surface roadway is the 1830 plat's Market Street; the same two nodes are shared with West Upper Wacker Drive, so which arm of the bend is named does not move the control.

randolph_canal.derived_from: read from OpenStreetMap 2026-08-09 for the Western Hotel placement; re-derived 2026-08-10 by tools/refetch_control.py --discover and CORRECTED
randolph_canal.note: GAP CLOSED 2026-08-10, AND THIS ONE MOVED 4.44 m. Randolph and Canal is a single crossing node in OpenStreetMap — the two street centrelines meet once — and it sits at E 446917.46, N 4637144.61, which is 2.14 m west and 3.89 m south of the coordinate committed on 2026-08-09. That older number cannot be reproduced from the two streets alone. What reproduces it, to 0.04 m, is the mean of FOUR nodes: the street crossing plus the three crossings the Canal Street and Randolph Street BIKEWAYS make with each other and with the roadways. That reading is inferred rather than recorded — nobody wrote the query down, which is the whole cost of the missing ids — but it is not a guess about a coincidence: the same inclusion is visible in `kinzie_canal`, whose five committed nodes include two Kinzie Street Bikeway crossings, and a name query written as a substring match ('Canal Street' matching 'Canal Street Bikeway') produces exactly this at both junctions and produces nothing extra at the other two, where no bikeway is mapped. A bikeway is drawn a few metres off the roadway it follows, so averaging one in moves the junction centre off the streets whose module the plat is about. The road-only reading is therefore adopted, the Western Hotel is moved with it, and the correction is 4.44 m against a georeference that carries ±20 m — an order of magnitude inside the uncertainty already declared, and now re-fetchable by anyone. The node was last edited 2024-05-01, so this is a correction to our reading, not a change in the city.

road_only_reading.derived: 2026-08-10, tools/refetch_control.py --discover, under the road-only half of `node_rule` above: the three of the five committed nodes that are West Kinzie Street x North Canal Street, averaged. The other two are the Kinzie Street Bikeway crossing Canal, about 6 m north of the roadway.
used_by: data/structures/north_branch_bridge.json phases[0].position.derivation — the deck centreline northing, which declares the 2.93 m difference from `utm_n` above as `centreline.control_variance_m`
data/streets/1835.json streets[canal].path_local_enu_m — the drawn line, whose own note says it uses this reading and not the five-node mean
road_only_reading.note: COMMITTED AS DATA BY T-0421, 2026-09-13, because it was load-bearing while living only in prose. Until now this coordinate existed in three paragraphs — `queued_correction` below, the bridge's derivation note, and docs/RESEARCH/street_module_1830.md § 3 — and two committed placements stood on it. Nothing could re-derive either of them, and nothing could measure what the queued correction would cost. `tools/measure_canal_control_spread.py` now does both off this field, and tools/check.sh runs it. THIS IS NOT A SECOND CONTROL POINT. `utm_e`/`utm_n` above stay the control: this entry is georeferencing GCP HB, and re-deriving it re-runs the Hathaway fit. This field is what the correction WOULD move the junction to, carried beside it so the cost is a number rather than an adjective.

kinzie_canal.queued_correction: THE 3.8 m IS NO LONGER A MYSTERY, 2026-08-10. Two of the five nodes above — 11851144367 and 11851144368 — are not Kinzie × Canal at all: they are where the KINZIE STREET BIKEWAY crosses Canal Street, about 6 m north of the roadway crossing. Under the road-only rule now stated in `node_rule`, this junction is the other three nodes, whose mean is E 446891.71, N 4637657.80 — which is the North Branch bridge's 2026-08-10 reading to 0.01 m. So the two coordinates were never two subsets chosen at random: one applied the rule and one did not. This entry keeps the five-node mean anyway, and the reason is cost, not doubt. It is georeferencing GCP HB, so re-deriving it re-runs the Hathaway cross-check fit, and it is the bridge's control, so moving it re-derives the deck's span from the traced banks and re-bakes the bridge — a Blender slice and a datum slice in one, which is not this slice. The variance stays declared on the bridge (data/structures/north_branch_bridge.json) and the correction stays queued with its cost written down. AND THE CORRECTION HAS A SECOND COST, MEASURED BY T-0421 ON 2026-09-13 AND SMALLER THAN IT LOOKS. Because this entry keeps the five-node mean, `tools/plat_corridors.py control_offsets()` reads Canal Street as the one street whose control does not agree with itself: lake_canal +0.00 m, randolph_canal +0.09 m, kinzie_canal -2.24 m, a spread of 2.33 m, verdict `disagree`, so Canal's platted corridor stays on the drawn line. Substitute `road_only_reading` above and the same computation returns +0.01, +0.00 and +0.09 — a spread of 0.09 m. THE 2.33 m IS THIS ENTRY'S BIKEWAY AND NOT CANAL STREET DISAGREEING WITH ITSELF: the drawn line reproduces all three of its control points to 9 cm once the cycle path is out of the average, which is what the `canal` record in data/streets/1835.json has said in words since it was drawn. The verdict does not change either way (0.09 m is still over the 0.01 m the offsets are quoted to) and so nothing moves; what changes is that the number is now derived rather than feared. tools/measure_canal_control_spread.py, run by tools/check.sh.
kinzie_canal.note: TWO COORDINATES FOR ONE JUNCTION EXIST IN THIS DATASET AND THIS IS THE OLDER AND BETTER-RECORDED ONE. The georeference took the mean of the five shared nodes above on 2026-08-09. The North Branch bridge's placement note describes reading the same junction on 2026-08-10 from 'three shared nodes', giving 41.889068 N, -87.640156 W = E 446891.7, N 4637657.8 — 3.8 m away, and its deck centreline stands on that second reading. Which subset of a five-node crossing you average is a choice nobody recorded making, and averaging a different subset of the same crossing is not a disagreement about where Kinzie and Canal is. The bridge declares the variance rather than absorbing it (data/structures/north_branch_bridge.json), because its span is a mesh parameter derived from where the deck meets the traced 1834 banks: moving the deck 2.9 m north re-derives the span and re-bakes the bridge, which is a slice with a Blender in it and not a bookkeeping edit. See docs/RESEARCH/street_module_1830.md § 3.

south_water_franklin.derived_from: read from OpenStreetMap 2026-08-28 under `node_rule`, reproducible with tools/refetch_control.py --discover south_water_franklin; the junction was first read 2026-08-27 by T-0183 while the Market x South Water refusal below was being recorded, and committed by T-0245
south_water_franklin.note: THE FIRST CONTROL POINT ANYWHERE ON SOUTH WATER STREET, and it is a crossing rather than the bend `refused_control.market_south_water` records one block west. The two shared nodes are Franklin's crossings of Wacker Drive's two carriageways, 15.28 m apart on the same easting to 0.08 m: 28358941 at E 447281.12 N 4637399.57 and 28358883 at E 447281.20 N 4637414.85. AND BOTH NAMED WAYS CONTINUE THROUGH THEM, which is the test the bend at Market fails and the thing a shared-node count cannot tell you on its own. North Franklin Street arrives from the south on way 452188414 (local 208.2, -12.3), passes through 28358941, runs on to 28358883 on way 253745133 and carries north beyond it; West Upper Wacker Drive crosses it east-west on a different carriageway at each node — way 319358165 in from the west and 931237159 out to the east through 28358941, way 319358163 in from the east and 1136945346 out to the west through 28358883. At Market neither holds: North Upper Wacker ENDS at the node and West Upper Wacker BEGINS there. The mean is local ENU (208.46, +11.41) off data/datum.json. It is also a corner this project already has a document about — the first post office stood at the south-west corner of Franklin and South Water from 2 Nov 1832 to 3 Mar 1837 (docs/research/03-structures-north.md), so it is on the scene date. WHAT IT CHANGED: NOTHING MOVED, AND THESE ARE THE NUMBERS, because the value of this point is that it makes two committed lines checkable for the first time rather than that it corrects them. data/streets/1835.json puts the South Water x Franklin corner at local (208.49, +2.83) — the intersection of the two committed centrelines — which is 8.58 m from this control, and essentially all of it is northing: dE -0.03 m, dN +8.58 m. So the whole disagreement is ACROSS South Water and none of it is along it. Franklin's committed centreline reproduces this junction's easting to 0.03 m, which is a reproduction and not an independent confirmation — `franklin` already lists `osm_streets_2026` among its sources. South Water's committed centreline stands 8.28 m SOUTH of the junction measured perpendicular to its own line (it runs 15.4 degrees north of east through this block). That southward stand is the deliberate one data/streets/1835.json describes as 'shifted into the dry half of the platted riverfront corridor', and after 2026-08-28 it is a measured 8.28 m rather than a sentence: 68 per cent of the 12.192 m half of the 80 ft platted module, so if the corridor is centred on this junction the reconstructed line sits inside its dry half with 3.91 m to spare before the south edge. Nothing is re-derived against this point and no placement names it: the standoff is a reconstruction decision about dry ground, not an error in an offset, and re-deriving South Water onto the modern centreline would undo it. See T-0245.

refused_control._doc: Junctions this project has LOOKED FOR under `node_rule` and could not make. A refusal is recorded here rather than left as an absence, because an absence reads as 'nobody has got to this one yet' and these are 'somebody did, and the rule cannot deliver it'. Each entry carries the same `osm_ways` a control point carries plus the centre the map extract was taken around, so `tools/refetch_control.py --discover <id>` re-runs the reading and anybody can check it against today's OpenStreetMap. They carry NO coordinate on purpose: a refused junction has no committed position, and writing one down anyway is the exact fault the refusal is about.

market_south_water.wanted_for: blk_south_water_market — north South Water, south Lake, west Market, east Franklin, 27 roofs of headroom. tools/generate_plat_lots.py refuses it because South Water's committed centreline stops 24 m short of Market's east block edge, and tools/measure_block_gating.py measures that run DRY (0 of 5 samples wet), so the block is real ground waiting on a trace rather than a product artifact.

reading.note: The map extract was taken around Market's easting 110 m north of Lake — where the plat puts the corner. Under node_rule the two named surface roadways share exactly two nodes, 28358888 and 28358944, and they are lake_market's own committed pair to the id: the same coordinate, the same 17.68 m spread, already in this file. The way geometry says why. North Upper Wacker Drive's northernmost way (931237154) ENDS at node 28358944; West Upper Wacker Drive's first way (319358162) BEGINS at it and runs north-east up to E 447213.3 N 4637344.7, and its other carriageway (319358170) comes back down to 28358888. The two arms are one carriageway pair changing name through a bend at the Lake Street junction, not two streets crossing at South Water.

market_south_water.verdict: THE RULE CANNOT MAKE THIS POINT, AND THE INTERESTING PART IS THAT IT DOES NOT FAIL LOUDLY. It returns two shared nodes with a clean mean and nothing in the output says they are a bend; committed as control, market_south_water would sit at local (89.16, -110.42) — ON Lake Street, 110 m south of the corner it names — and the block it was fetched to unlock would be built with zero depth. The reason is not that the modern city lost the corner but that it lost the STREET: Wacker Drive only reaches South Water's line (about local N +5 to +11) at Franklin, 120 m east of Market, and west of Franklin it turns south-west onto the Lake and Market corner instead of running on to a Market intersection. So there is no modern crossing to read here, and widening node_rule to admit a bend node would not produce the right answer — it would commit a wrong one. What South Water's west approach already stands on is not modern control at all: data/streets/1835.json records that stretch as following 'the dry south bank resolved by the committed heightfield'.
market_south_water.what_would_settle_it: An owner decision, not a steward one, and it is no longer the question T-0183 opened with. Not 'may a bend node be control' — that answer is measured and it is no — but: may South Water Street's committed west end be CLOSED onto Market's corridor from the 1834 sheets and the committed bank, the same basis the rest of that curve already stands on, with the corner graded for what it is; or should blk_south_water_market's 27 roofs stop being scheduled as gated on street control and go back to the South balance, the way blk_south_water_clinton's did when T-0163 measured them?
market_south_water.not_the_same_as: South Water Street is not without derivable control everywhere — only here. The same extract, same rule, reads 'West Upper Wacker Drive' x 'North Franklin Street' as a clean two-node crossing: 28358941 (E 447281.12, N 4637399.57) and 28358883 (E 447281.20, N 4637414.85), mean E 447281.16, N 4637407.21, spread 15.28 m, local (208.46, +11.41) — 6.4 m north of Franklin's committed north end, and the corner the first post office stood on from 2 Nov 1832 to 3 Mar 1837. It is measured here and deliberately NOT adopted: committing the dataset's first control point on South Water re-derives placements and is its own unit of work, not a footnote on a refusal.
market_south_water.the_owner_ruled_and_the_ground_refused_i: THE RULING CAME ON 2026-08-29 AND IT CANNOT BE EXECUTED ON THE LINE AS COMMITTED. Asked the question above, the owner chose the first branch: close South Water Street's west end onto Market's corridor from the 1834 sheets and the committed bank, the same basis the rest of that curve already stands on, graded for what it is. T-0183 carried that out and measured what it does. IT DOES NOT OPEN THE BLOCK. South Water's committed west approach bends south onto the dry bank at Wolf Point and has CONVERGED ON LAKE STREET before it gets to Market: its drawn west end (100, -101) stands 9.5 m from Lake's committed centreline, so the two 24.384 m platted corridors already overlap by 14.9 m there. Close the end onto Market's corridor and the four crossings tools/generate_plat_lots.py needs are all found — and blk_south_water_market is emitted as a BOWTIE, its north-west corner 14.9 m SOUTH of its south-west one, reported with an area of 4,411 m2 and a depth of 36.85 m. That is node_rule's own failure mode one layer down: an answer that looks right rather than no answer, this time out of the street layer instead of OpenStreetMap. tools/generate_plat_lots.py now refuses a block whose rows have crossed, and tools/check.sh fires that refusal on this very case (--self-test).
market_south_water.and_the_ground_is_the_reason_not_the_dra: The tempting reply is that the committed west approach is simply drawn too far south and a better line would open the block. It would not, and the heightfield says so. At Market's easting the committed south bank of the main stem stands at local N -71.0, and Lake Street's north corridor edge at local N -98.2. Carry South Water as far north as that ground allows — its north corridor edge exactly ON the waterline, no margin at all — and its south corridor edge lands at N -95.4: 2.8 m of block depth at Market, against the 24.384 m a single platted lot fronts. Measured east of there the same way: 7.2 m at E +100, 22.5 m at E +110, 37.6 m at E +120, 86.4 m at Franklin. So the block is not a rectangle waiting on a trace; it is a wedge the South Branch pinches out at its west corner, and no derivation of the closure can put a lot in the first fifteen metres of it. The 27 roofs tools/reconcile_665.py schedules against this block are not on the ground the ruling was about. That 2.8 m is gated: tools/generate_plat_lots.py --self-test re-derives it from the committed heightfield on every commit and fails if it ever exceeds a lot's frontage.
market_south_water.what_would_settle_it_now: Still the owner's, and it is a third option neither branch of the 2026-08-29 question offered, because nobody had measured the pinch: blk_south_water_market can be built ONLY as a wedge that tapers to nothing at Market, on a west approach re-derived north onto the waterline with no clearance — which moves a committed centreline up to 34 m and re-scores every gate that reads it. Is that wedge worth having, or do the block's 27 roofs go back to the South balance the way blk_south_water_clinton's did when T-0163 measured them? The measurement is in tools/generate_plat_lots.py --self-test and in docs/RESEARCH/thompson_plat_grid.md § 6.2.
